Untrue, thankfully. Even if everyone in Congress unanimously agreed to amend the Constitution, they cannot do so on their own. Two thirds of them must propose the amendment, and then three fourths of the states must ratify it in order for it to become law.
Why doesn't the US require a referendum to modify the constitution like most other countries I know about?

The people who wrote the US Constitution wanted it to be incredibly difficult to amend, such that it would only be changed when almost everyone agreed that the amendment was necessary. Most countries allow either a simple majority of its legislature (Australia, South Africa, Belgium, France, etc.) or a simple majority by referendum.

The US, as I mentioned, requires not only two thirds of Congress to approve it (a rare occurrence on anything), but also for the legislatures of three fourths of the states. To the best of my knowledge, it's either the most difficult or very nearly the most difficult Constitution to amend.

Australia is most certainly not a simple majority of the legislature! It's a referendum which requires not only an overall majority but also a majority in at least four out of six states.

This makes changing the constitution very hard indeed, and that's a good thing.

The US model requires only the political class to agree on something. Makes it too easy to change. Example: banning alcohol was not a good move.

Across the Cosmos Podcast: Episode 45 - The Organic Church

It is called the “Simple Church,” the “Organic Church,” the “Book of Acts Church,” the “Primitive Church,” the “House Church” and the “Micro-Church.” What I am talking about is a gathering of people of usually the Christian faith who meet together in small groups of no more than 15 to 20 people in one another’s homes or in some location by which they can worship Christ and fellowship together. To these people, these gatherings are their version of Church.

This type of “church experience” is a foreign concept to most Christians – or to most any who regard themselves as people of faith world-wide. Irrespective the faith, all who subscribe to a “higher power” generally worship in the exact same manner and style. It is the one commonality amongst ALL faiths world-wide. However Jesus Christ did not instruct his disciples to teach others this hierarchal manner of worship, preferring instead a more intimate, familial approach.

Those who have adopted the Organic or Home Church model are not part of the traditional orthodox church structure. They do not attend church in a fixed building, listen to a pastor opine behind a pulpit, or sit mute in a pew for 45 minutes to an hour and a half once a week. They do not stop and pray five times a day in order to please an ill-tempered god. In the Organic Church, all who take part are also active participants. This is a stark departure from traditional or orthodox church services we are all familiar with regardless the faith.

Join Chase Rockwell, Lou Rodgers and Dave Cameron as they explore this purest form of Christian worship and whether it is possible today.
